cues.text: Section three: benchmarking and performance frameworks.
Benchmarking compares performance against a meaningful reference, so that an organisation can identify opportunities for improvement.
There are several kinds of benchmarking.
Internal benchmarking compares teams, branches or periods within a single organisation.
Competitive benchmarking compares direct competitors, where comparable data is available.
Functional benchmarking compares similar functions across different industries.
Generic benchmarking, also called best-practice benchmarking, examines effective practices regardless of the industry in which they are found.
Consider a bank.
It might compare transaction latency across its own branches.
It might compare its service availability against industry targets.
And it might study the incident-management practices of a telecom operator.
In every case, the comparison must account for workload, service scope, geography, measurement methods and customer needs.
Without that care, the comparison can mislead.
The benchmarking cycle runs as follows.
First, define objectives.
Second, select metrics and comparison partners.
Third, collect comparable data.
Fourth, analyse the gaps.
Fifth, implement improvements.
And finally, reassess.
One caution matters here: a benchmark is not automatically an appropriate target.
A rural clinic and a global payment processor operate under very different constraints, so the same figure cannot sensibly be demanded of both.
Now to the Balanced Scorecard.
It connects operational measures to strategic outcomes through four perspectives.
Let us take the table row by row.
The first perspective is Financial.
An IT example is cost per transaction, and return on investment, or ROI.
The second is the Customer perspective.
Here the examples are satisfaction and successful transactions.
The third is Internal processes.
The examples are incident restoration time and deployment quality.
The fourth is Learning and growth.
The examples are staff skills and improvement capability.
These perspectives interact.
Take a fintech.
Training its engineers in reliability practices can improve its recovery processes.
Better recovery improves customer trust, and it also reduces revenue lost to outages.
So an investment in learning and growth ends up showing in the customer and financial perspectives.
Frameworks also support this work.
COBIT supports governance and performance assessment.
ITIL supports service improvement.
ISO-based management systems establish structured requirements and review processes.
These frameworks help organise measurement, but none of them eliminates the need to select meaningful indicators.
Finally, efficiency and effectiveness.
Efficiency means achieving outputs with minimal waste, cost or time.
Effectiveness means achieving the intended objective.
Consider a support desk that closes tickets quickly but fails to solve customer problems.
It is efficient only by a misleading measure.
Here is a numerical example.
Suppose a team processes 1,000 transactions at a cost of ₦50,000.
The cost per transaction is ₦50.
After optimisation, it processes 1,250 transactions at the same cost.
The unit cost falls to ₦40, which is a 20% reduction.
However, if errors rise significantly, effectiveness may have declined despite the improved unit cost.
